Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The truth is that the soul and body are necessarily linked, but not as two relative things, nor as two effects of the same cause with no bond between them. They are linked like matter and form. Each needs the other in its own way, without an impossible circular dependence. The body needs the soul—not one particular soul, but a soul in general—in order to be a living body. The soul needs the body only for its particular, individual existence and for its coming to be as a soul.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world
With this in mind, we can say that the soul comes before the body by nature.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world
Someone may say: if so, the body cannot end unless the soul ends too.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

I reply: that is right for the body considered as a body. A body cannot exist as a living body while its soul exists in it, or continue as that same living body once the soul is gone. What remains after the soul departs is no longer that body, but matter or a different kind of body. The living body as such depends on its soul. The soul and body are causes of one another in different ways.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Nor can someone object that, if the soul causes the body, it must depend on the body in order to act. Matter does not help the source that gives it its own form to act on it. If the soul could act without any dependence on matter, then it would no longer be a soul but an intellect.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

We reply that every form, whether it exists in matter or acts through matter, affects the matter and its conditions together with a separate source. It does not act independently or in one particular form, but together with the source beyond it, according to its nature in general. The soul, as a general kind of soul, remains one and acts as a cause that sustains the body. But each particular soul depends on the body for the features that make it an individual, just as a form depends on matter for its particular states.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

As for the objection that the body cannot be the soul’s cause because the soul is immaterial, we reply that an immaterial intellect is something that acts without any relation to bodies. The soul is not like that. The argument works if it is applied to an intellect that exists intellectually in itself and has no relation to bodies at all. Such an intellect does not perish when a body perishes. But intellect as a separate being is not the same as a soul that governs a particular body and is changed and completed through it.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The body is not simply a tool that the soul picks up and puts down, like a carpenter using a chisel or a saw. Nor is the soul in the body like a captain in a ship or a homeowner in a house: the ship and house remain what they are whether the captain or owner is there or not. These arguments do not prove that the soul, while it exists as a soul, continues after the body. They prove only that a separate intellect does not perish with the body. The remaining question is whether some or all souls change into a being that no longer depends on a body or uses it for completion. We will soon see how this change happens.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

As for the philosophers’ claim that a cause untouched by change can act only when a condition appears, and that the condition for something’s beginning is not needed for its continued existence, this is mistaken. Coming to be is not a feature added to a thing’s existence; it is simply that existence after nonexistence. The condition for its coming to be is therefore also a condition for its existence. When the condition is gone, so is the thing that depends on it.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Nor does it make sense to say that matter can prepare or provide a condition for the existence of a substance that is separate from matter and needs no matter or material conditions. In general, matter can prepare only for what can become one of its states. There is no sense in saying that something can be prepared for a being whose nature is entirely different from its own. Keep this question in mind, for it will come up again.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world
Earlier, we argued that the soul cannot be destroyed when the body is destroyed. Here, we make a stronger claim: the soul cannot perish at all.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Two arguments support this. First, the soul is something that can exist, and everything that can exist has a cause. As long as that cause remains, together with all the things that make it a cause, its effect cannot cease. We have explained this in the discussion of cause and effect. If the soul could cease to exist, it would have to be because its cause—or one part of its complete cause—had ceased.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

There are four kinds of cause: what brings a thing about, what it is made from, the form that makes it what it is, and its end or purpose. The soul cannot perish because its maker disappears. As we will show, its maker is an intellect entirely separate from matter, and the same argument applies to that intellect: it cannot perish. Nor can the soul perish because its material cause disappears, since the soul is not material but immaterial. Nor can it perish because its form disappears, since the soul's form is its very nature. If that form could disappear, we would face the same question about the soul itself. If a second form were needed to explain why the first disappeared, that second form would need another form, and so on without end. The soul cannot perish because its end or purpose disappears either. So the soul cannot perish at all.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

By contrast, forms and qualities that can disappear do so because one of their causes, even the cause that brings them about, can disappear. Their immediate causes are temporary: they arise from different mixtures in the body, and those mixtures create different conditions for them. We have already shown that the soul does not arise in this way.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The second argument begins with the claim that anything new must first be able to exist. If it could not, then it would be impossible, and what is impossible cannot exist. If something became new without first being able to become new, it would not really be new at all, which is a contradiction. By “able to exist,” we mean that it is fully ready to exist. Such readiness must belong to something that can receive it: the thing that is close to coming into being must have a basis that can support it.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

If the soul could perish, there would have to be something that could hold the possibility of its perishing. That cannot be the soul itself, because the soul would not remain as it perished. Yet whatever holds this possibility must remain while the soul perishes. So the soul would have to have matter. We would then ask the same question about that matter. If it could perish, it too would need matter, and this would continue without end. If the chain ends, something must remain that cannot perish. That would be part of the soul. It could not have a position or occupy space, since then the soul would also have a position and occupy space, and could not receive intellectual forms. But what we have shown must remain is without position or place and can receive intellectual forms. That is exactly what we mean by the soul: an immaterial being able to understand. So the soul cannot perish.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Someone might ask: does the soul not have matter that holds the possibility of its coming into being? Why could that matter not also hold the possibility of the soul's perishing? The difference is this: the body can remain as the soul comes into being. But if the body held the possibility of the soul's perishing, it would have to remain after the soul perished. Everyone agrees that the body does not remain when the soul is gone.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Still, these arguments prove only that a simple being whose existence is wholly separate from matter cannot be destroyed. They do not prove that an existence tied to the body can survive the body's destruction. If the soul exists only through its connection to the body, that connected existence would not survive the body's end. But it could not have begun when the body began either, nor could it have been renewed as the body arose. In that case, it would never truly be new. The same individual existence cannot both begin as part of matter and be separate from matter, unless it changes deeply in its very being and becomes separate after first being tied to matter.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The remaining question is how the soul's separate existence can begin if a separate being has no tie to matter and no material readiness to exist. We will answer this later. For now, we can say this: the soul does not become separate by gaining a new, immaterial existence. Rather, its existence through its connection to the body comes to an end, and it returns to its original source. In truth, something becomes separate when a new relation to it begins. This is like the soul's memory faculty coming into being as a storehouse for what it understands.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The argument that the body holds the possibility of the soul's coming into being, but not the possibility of its perishing, also trades on two meanings of “receiver.” Sometimes this means something ready to receive a form; sometimes it means something that is acted on or completed by a form. The body that holds the possibility of the soul's coming into being is not the living body, but something earlier, such as the seed from which the body's parts develop. That earlier thing does not remain when the soul-form comes into being. The body that remains with the soul receives it in another sense: the soul completes the body, as the form completes the material part of a living thing. The body may also be what receives the possibility of the soul's perishing; but the thing that can receive that perishing is something else, something that remains when the soul is gone. For both coming into being and perishing, we must distinguish what a thing comes from and what it exists in. If we ignore the difference, we confuse the two cases.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world
VI. An Eastern account of the soul's return
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The distinguished scholar Nasir al-Din Muhammad al-Tusi once wrote to one of his learned contemporaries, Shams al-Din al-Khusrawshahi, and asked him to explain several difficult questions. His correspondent did not answer. One of the unanswered questions concerned whether the soul survives after the body dies. Al-Tusi put it this way:
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

“Why do those who say that a thing cannot come into being or perish unless there is something that can hold the possibility of its coming or going say that the human soul comes into being but cannot perish? If the body holds the possibility of the soul's coming into being, why does it not also hold the possibility of its perishing? If the soul has no basis for the possibility of perishing because it is separate from matter, why does that same reason not mean it has no basis for the possibility of coming into being? Then it could never begin. How can a material body hold the possibility of a being free of matter, so different from itself? If the body holds this possibility because the soul is the body's particular form, why does it not also hold the possibility of the soul's nonexistence for that very reason? Why are the two cases treated differently, when their relation to the body seems the same?”
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world
This clear statement shows that al-Tusi was not satisfied with the answers he found in books, even in his own commentary on Ibn Sina's Remarks and Admonitions.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

We answered this question earlier. The human body, through its special readiness, calls on the Giver of Forms for a form that will govern it and act within it, preserving both the individual and the human kind. But a form that can guide human life and sustain the body's balanced condition must have a spiritual power: it must perceive, reason, think, and distinguish. So the generous source gives the soul and its true nature.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The body's readiness asks only for a form that is present with it and acts in it as its form. But the generosity of the source gives a form that also has a separate nature, or a separate source. One thing can be a substance in one respect and a quality in another. For example, a form understood by the mind is a substance by its nature, but as it exists in the mind it depends on the mind and is a mental quality. A thing can also be caused in one respect but not in another: its existence is caused, while its nature is not. In the same way, the human soul can be immaterial in its nature, as an intellect, and material in how it acts by governing the body. Insofar as it acts on the body, its coming into being depends on the body's readiness, and it ceases when the body does. But in its original nature, or in the source of its nature, it does not depend on the body's readiness except indirectly, and it does not perish when the body perishes. The limits of material things touch it only indirectly.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

That was our earlier answer, reached through rational argument. Here is the answer I now offer: the human soul has several levels of being. Some belong to the world of divine command and direction—“Say: The spirit is from the command of my Lord.” Others belong to the world of creation and shaping—“From it We created you, to it We return you, and from it We bring you out.” Coming into being and change apply only to some of the soul's levels.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The soul develops and passes from one level of existence to another. The Qur'an points to this when it says, “We created you, then shaped you, then said to the angels, ‘Bow before Adam.’” When the soul rises from the world of creation to the world of command, its existence becomes an intellect separate from matter. It no longer needs the body, its conditions, or its readiness. The body's loss of readiness can affect the soul's connection to the body and its activity through it, but not the soul's own nature or continued existence.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The soul's existence when it first comes into being is not the same as its existence when it continues. The first depends on matter; the second is separate from it. The soul is therefore bodily in how it begins and spiritual in how it continues. A child needs the womb at first but not later. A captured animal needs the net to be caught, but not to remain alive after it has been caught. The body's decay, like the womb's or net's, does not prevent the child or captured animal from continuing to exist.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Also, a thing's need for something does not mean that everything belonging to it by its nature needs that same thing. A caused existence needs a cause, but a thing's nature need not. The existence of a triangle is caused, but its having three angles is not.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

A preparatory cause is a cause only indirectly. Its role is not like that of a necessary cause, whose loss would bring about the effect's loss. The rule that something without a basis for the possibility of existence or nonexistence cannot begin after it was absent or end after it existed does not mean that something without a basis for possible existence cannot exist again after it has already existed. Its earlier existence may be enough to support its later existence, if the later existence is a new and fuller stage of the earlier one.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

In a gradual change, such as a color growing deeper or a coal becoming hotter, the readiness for each weaker stage disappears, but the thing itself remains and grows stronger. What vanishes is its weakness and lack. So in a movement toward completion, the loss of a thing's readiness does not always end its existence. It may change into a stronger and more complete existence. In the same way, when the body loses its readiness for the soul, the soul's bodily mode ends, but that does not mean the soul becomes nothing.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

If someone asks how the soul's separate existence begins when everything new must have matter and what is separate from matter has none, the answer is that the new thing is not the separate intellect itself. What begins is the soul's connection with that intellect and its transformation into it. That connection is preceded by readiness. While the soul is tied to the body, it holds the possibility of this connection. Once it unites with the intellect, it holds the actual connection. As we have said, what holds the possibility of something need not be what holds that thing's completed existence, though the two cannot be wholly separate.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The philosophers who study divine things say that every natural kind has a built-in movement toward its own end, and that every incomplete thing has an inborn desire for completion. When a thing reaches its completion, it unites with it and becomes something new. The human being's natural movement toward holiness is clear to anyone who can see it. When the soul reaches the level of intellect, it becomes pure intellect and joins the Active Intellect. It then becomes the Active Intellect. What had been a soul capable of understanding, but not yet fully understanding, now leaves matter behind. Its unrealized capacities fall away, and it remains through God.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

In short, we can fully understand this only if we understand how the soul joins the Active Intellect and how all things return to the Highest Source. The stages of being follow one another and differ in strength, yet remain connected. The end of one level is the beginning of the next. The last step of existence tied to the body is the first step of existence separate from matter. The world that is wholly separate from matter contains no coming into being, change, or new states. The soul's entry into that world does not change it, just as the soul's coming from it did not change it. The soul enters that world in the same way it came from it, without any change taking place in that world. Think carefully about this and the meaning will become clear.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world
VII. The rational soul comes from an intellect separate from matter
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

We have already shown that the cause of souls cannot be a body simply because it is a body. If it could, every body would be a cause of souls. Nor can the cause be a power that depends on a body. Such a power either needs the body in order to exist, or it exists without depending on the body but needs the body only to act. Both possibilities are impossible. So such a power cannot cause the soul to exist.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The first possibility is impossible for several reasons. First, a bodily form can act only in cooperation with what receives its action, and that receiver is the body. Then the body would be part of the cause that produces the soul, which is impossible, as we have already explained. Second, a bodily form acts through its position: position is part of the way a body exists. But a body cannot have a position in relation to something that has no position.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Third, a cause must be fuller and stronger than its effect. A body depends on matter for its existence, while an immaterial being does not. So the cause of the soul cannot depend on a body for its own existence.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

The second possibility is also impossible. If a power needs a body only in order to act, the body must serve as a tool between that power and what it affects. A body can serve as a tool only through its position and size. Its nearness to different things would vary, and so would its effects. To affect something, it would have to be near it to some degree. If nearness made no difference—if the power worked on nearby and distant things in exactly the same way—then the body would play no part in the action. A body's own existence and identity depend on its particular position. And if the action on a nearby thing happened before the action on a distant thing, then the action could be near or far. It would not be the action of an immaterial spirit. So anything that acts through a body has a position; and anything without a position cannot act through a body. Since the soul has no position, it cannot be caused by a body or through one. Its cause must be free of matter both in its own existence and in its action. It must be a sacred, separate being, whether a form or another soul. Philosophers call it the Active Intellect; ancient Persian sages called it rūwān-bakhsh, “giver of the spirit.”
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

It is called an intellect because it is a form separate from matter and understands itself. Every being separate from matter understands itself, and its knowledge of itself is its very existence. It is called “active” for three reasons. First, it gives existence to our souls and brings them from the ability to understand in principle to actual understanding. Second, it is fully active, without anything still only possible in it. It contains all intelligible things—or indeed all things—in intellectual form. Here, “active” also expresses the fullness of its activity. Third, it gives existence to this world and to the forms that enter matter. But it is not God, the Necessary Being, because it is the last of the separate intellects and contains some multiplicity. God is perfectly one; souls are many.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

Someone may ask: why can one soul not cause another, as a parent's soul might cause a child's? We answer that a soul acts through its relation to a body. It cannot act on something that has no position in relation to it.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

This is better than the argument Ibn Sina gives in The Discussions: souls belong to the same kind. If one soul caused another, either it would be one particular soul or several souls. If it were one particular soul, there would be no reason to choose it as the cause rather than the other soul. If it were an unspecified soul, it could not cause a particular soul, since a particular effect needs a particular cause. If several souls were the cause, there would be no reason to choose one number of souls rather than another. Then all the souls existing in the world would have to cause the new soul. But the smaller number of souls that existed earlier would already have been enough to cause it. If just one or a few of them were enough, the whole group would not be needed. Two separate causes that are each enough to produce the same effect cannot both be its cause. So the soul cannot be caused by all earlier souls together or by some of them rather than others.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

This argument assumes that all souls remain the same kind. In our view, souls can become different kinds as their habits and character grow firm—angelic, demonic, animal-like, or predatory. They may be one kind at the beginning, before their habits and knowledge have developed. If a soul whose character has become fully actual causes another soul, Ibn Sina's argument does not apply.
Book Seven: Aspects of the rational soul in its relation to the natural world

This completes the first part of the journey of the soul. The printed edition calls it the Fourth Journey. The handwritten copy used here, traced through other copies to the author's copy dated 1210 AH, calls it the Third Journey. That may fit better with the book's arrangement around the stages of the mystic's journey toward God. The editors worked hard to prepare and correct the text and to present it in a clear order. God is the giver of success and kindness. (Publisher)

By “source” here, the author means the receptive source: the beginning of formation in the world of becoming, which comes with substantial motion and the natural renewal of things. In the case of the four elements, this means their ongoing change and their relation to pure receptivity—the first matter, which is pure potential and is drawn toward forms. The elements and natural forms move by their very nature. Since first matter is pure potential, it cannot by itself actively cause the soul or anything else to exist; if it could, it would no longer be pure potential. Nor can the elements, as bodies, be the active cause that brings something from nonexistence into existence. A giver must possess what it gives in a higher way than the recipient does. The cause must therefore be higher in existence than its effect. The elements are lower in existence than the soul, so they cannot be its active cause. The active cause of the soul and of all the perfections that come to first matter and its earliest forms is God’s pure providence, flowing down through every level.

The soul’s unity, which is identical with its existence, is a distinctive kind of unity: a comprehensive unity that gathers many levels of being. In one respect it is many within one; in another, one within many. In its own nature, the soul has a single, unified existence, including the forms that appear through it. Its branches and dependent powers are spread through it, as it were, by a process of descent. Taken in its full sense, the soul includes both this unified existence and its many branches. Its origin is one of its levels: prior to it in time, but later than it in essence. The levels that come earlier in time are one with those that come later in essence, though they differ in the direction of their development. So the soul is low in its height and high in its lowliness; it is pure even while embodied, and embodied even while immaterial. It is present in its branches without being inside them as one thing is inside another, and beyond them without being outside them as one thing is outside another. “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.” Guard this insight from those who deny the mysteries of divine unity. The Imams have described it as a middle way between compulsion and complete freedom, between likeness and denial of likeness, and between negating God and comparing Him to created things.

“Possible” here means what can be brought into being by the Holy Emanation. Through the Most Holy Emanation, things are first measured out and given their timeless ordering. God’s providence is His knowledge of the best order before creation; that knowledge is active and brings what is known into existence. After His self-disclosure to Himself, God discloses Himself through His names and attributes and what follows from them, then through the individual things themselves. The first is His disclosure through the names and attributes, called the Most Holy Emanation; the second is His disclosure through the things that exist, called the Holy Emanation. The first is the mercy of His attributes, encompassing the intelligible meanings of things; the second is His active mercy, encompassing the existence of possible things.

If things were not brought into existence in this order, they would either all issue at once from the simple First Principle, which would mean that many things came from a source that is one in every respect, or they would issue in order with the least complete things first. The first option would make the First Principle composite; the second would make the lower things exist before the higher. Both are impossible. A cause must be most closely matched to its direct effect. If it were equally matched to several effects, there would be no reason for one rather than another to issue from it. The more complete thing is more closely matched to the cause than the less complete one. Also, the complete cause must contain in itself the full basis for its direct effect. If a lower effect came first and then caused the higher one, the First Cause would not fully account for the higher effect, and the cause would be less complete than its effect.
The reason is the one already given: if God’s providence stopped at a limit, His own being would be limited too. Far exalted is He above that.

“The first thing it received” follows from the earlier point that the outpouring cannot stop, or else the received thing would remain unchanged. The “rays” are an analogy for the giving of the generous First Principle through its intermediaries. The analogy is about how the effect spreads; the rays themselves are preparatory conditions, not active causes.
This gives an example of a sensible effect that even someone who relies only on the senses will recognize.

Matter is prepared for its kinds of perfection by its specific forms. Its specific perfections arise from those forms; its incidental readiness is an effect of its essential readiness. Matter is prepared by the forms it receives, not by itself, since as pure potential it is equally open to all perfections.

Strictly speaking, plants should not be called “living” in the sense of perceiving and acting: perception begins at least with touch, and action at least with movement by choice, neither of which plants have. It is true that existence itself is life flowing through all things, as the author insists elsewhere, though he criticizes Ibn Arabi for applying this idea to bodies in his discussion of the afterlife. But that broader sense does not fit this passage, where plants are distinguished from minerals and animals by the kind of life they have. Nor does it fit the phrase “the first thing matter receives,” which suggests that what came before plants lacked life in that sense.

A simple reality, such as necessary existence or existence in its absolute sense, has no source from which one could define it or prove it. One may still prove it through its effects or through the way it is affected, as one proves a reality from what it does. The same applies, even more clearly, to souls and forms. A form is another name for what makes a thing actual. A simple reality has no material or formal parts from which to define it or demonstrate it.

This follows the usual account. In the author’s own view, sensible things are perceived through the soul’s activity, and intelligible things through union with them and with the Active Intellect, as explained later.

One could say that the soul, as soul, is material and exists in the body, as the author himself holds. His point is that calling it a “form” does not show that it has another level of existence, while “perfection” does not imply that it must inhere in something. A king completes a city, for example, without being a form impressed in it. The author is also reporting the philosophers’ preferred wording.

The soul’s perfection was just compared to a kind, and a kind is closer to a general category because it can be predicated of its instances. Form, by contrast, is compared with matter, which is farther from a general category: matter is considered on its own as something distinct, while a general category is predicated of things. The point is that something whose comparison is closer to the general category is a better candidate for the broader term in a definition. One could turn this argument around: form may be closer to meaning, or even be the same as the general category, while kind and matter differ only in how they are considered. These are arguments about what seems most fitting, not decisive proofs.

Matter is included in the idea of form because form points to the matter it informs. The idea of perfection, by contrast, points to the kind it completes, and a kind may be bodily or separate from matter. Thus defining the soul through perfection can include material souls such as plant souls and souls that are separate in their own nature.

This objection applies only if the definition is meant for animal soul alone and “power” means the power of movement. It does not apply if the definition is for soul in general, whether plant or animal, and “power” is understood broadly.

The issue is that a cause may be favored over another without any reason. One might reply that “power” means actuality in a broad sense and applies to all souls. The author’s point, however, is that definitions are about realities, not just words, and the soul in general has no existence apart from its particular instances.

“Perfection” can be used with the same meaning for both powers: it can mean the completion provided by the power of movement or the completion provided by both powers, as in the animal soul. “Power,” by contrast, is used in two different senses. If both are used in a definition, the word is equivocal; if one is chosen, there is no reason to prefer one over the other, and the definition leaves out part of the soul. It also fails to describe the soul as a whole, since the animal soul includes both powers. The point is that one and the same word, “perfection,” can apply to both without changing its meaning.

This objection has force. “Perfection” means that the soul completes a kind, as explained earlier. Although in reality the soul can also be called a perfection in another sense—because its two powers are one in being—this does not follow from the word itself.
“Limited” here may mean limited by one of the soul’s levels and by the body, or limited by the two together, or limited by the relation described in the definition.
The definition points to the soul and is measured by it; it does not mean that existence itself has definitions, as if definitions belonged to existence rather than to what a thing is.
The active cause here is the First Cause, God, and the active intellects. Things that depend on causes can be known only through their causes.

The question is what the soul is. People have held many views. Some, following Galen and his school, say that the soul is the body’s temperament or mixture. As long as the body keeps the temperament suitable to its kind, it is protected from corruption; once it loses that balance, the body dies. Others, including the theologian Imām al-Ḥaramayn, say that the soul is a fine, luminous body flowing through the body as water flows through a flower or fire through a coal. They say that this subtle body is addressed, rewarded, and punished, and that the visible body is kept together by it; when it leaves, the visible body quickly falls apart. Most Muʿtazilites and some Ashʿarites say that the soul is the visible body itself. Naẓẓām says it is an indivisible part located in the heart. In short, theologians have held nearly forty views, none supported by decisive proof. The most familiar is that the soul consists of original bodily parts that remain from the beginning to the end of life. It is astonishing that anyone who claims to follow reason would accept such accounts. The truth is what careful philosophers and mystics who have direct insight have taught: the soul is an immaterial substance that governs and preserves the body. Proofs will follow. A person can also test this by reflecting on the elements—earth, water, fire, and air—from which every bodily being is formed. Imagine the human being returned to those elements and set beside the elements outside the body. Could reason attribute the knowledge, wisdom, and power that make a fully developed human being God’s representative to earth, water, fire, air, or their mixture? No. Search within the earth and you will find a precious substance: a divine command and a sacred mystery. The author will later report the ancient philosophers’ views from Avicenna’s The Healing and interpret them.

The point is that it is false to say the soul’s true nature cannot be known from this definition. From the beginning, the soul is this relation to the body, and this relation is one level of its own being. The claim that it is a separate substance in its essence but related to the body only in its activity is wrong from the outset. If it existed before the body, that would be false; if it began to exist later, it would have no subject in which to begin, as will be explained.

A definition “by name alone” does not include a real nature. For example, the descriptions “black” and similar derived words do not correspond to one further thing in the world. “Black” refers to a body, which is a substance, and blackness, which is a quality; there is no third entity corresponding to the word. A definition of this kind does not include a distinct nature.

The exception is not quite of the same kind. The soul’s movement from bodily nature toward the Active Intellect is a strengthening of existence, one level after another. The soul that reaches the level of intellect preserves its earlier level as soul.

Most philosophers hold that the soul’s connection with the body follows from its coming into existence, rather than belonging to its nature. They also do not think it impossible for an immaterial and a material thing to form one kind. So neither premise in the two arguments is accepted by them. Both premises must be established for the arguments to work.

One might object that the proof applies only if the soul’s nature necessarily requires a body, while the soul might be eternal or might have begun before the body. The author replies that the point is the conflict between saying the soul is a separate intellectual substance and saying it is connected to matter. There is also a problem if the soul is new: what subject could have received it? The argument does not depend on the word “then” meaning a later moment in time. In any case, the soul’s eternity has already been disproved. If someone says that a soul that comes into being must also perish, we answer that the soul’s bodily coming into being does not prevent its continued existence as a spirit.

There are two kinds of relation. In one, the relation is part of what a thing is, or its nature is nothing but that relation; this is a category of relation. In the other, a thing’s nature belongs to another category, but its existence involves a relation. Matter, for example, is a substance by nature, though its existence involves a relation; blackness is a quality by nature, though its existence is entirely dependent on a subject. God has no created nature or category, yet descriptions such as creator and powerful apply to Him. The same distinction appears in things that flow or change. Motion and time are flowing by their very nature, while qualities, quantities, place, position, and natural forms may be stable in what they are but flowing in their existence. In one way or another, the physical world, with all its substances and accidents, is changing and passing away.

The author uses this as a proof that existence is fundamental. If existence were only an idea drawn from things, blackness would be nothing but its particular nature. But blackness exists only as the existence of a subject; it is therefore a relation in its existence, even if it is a quality by nature.
That is, separate from the body which the soul governs and completes.
Earlier statements by the author point to this: the soul’s relation to the body follows from its relation of governing and acting on bodies; he also says that the soul is the body’s completion.
A kind counts as an actual kind when it has the active source of these actions; it does not have to be carrying them all out. Having the power and source of the actions is enough.

At first this may seem to conflict with the author’s claim elsewhere that we use a description such as “knower” only when the thing actually has knowledge. One way to resolve the issue is to say that an “actual geometer” is someone who actually has the capacity to measure, and an “actual doctor” someone who actually has the capacity to treat. We do not call someone “treating” while they only have the capacity to treat. There is a difference between being actually an animal or a geometer, and actually sensing, acting, or measuring.

The soul is the first perfection of a body taken with an additional condition—that it be a plant, animal, or human being. But for body considered simply as body, without that condition, the soul is a later perfection, perhaps even a third one after elemental and mineral forms. If body is taken as something separate from all these forms, the soul is not its perfection at all.

The soul is not the first perfection of an animal considered without qualification, and may not be any perfection of it if the animal is taken as a complete kind already constituted. The soul is a first perfection of an animal only when it is considered with the condition that it can receive the soul. The same applies to the soul in relation to body generally. The author later says that the soul is the first perfection of body considered without qualification; he means body without a restriction that would exclude its becoming a plant, animal, or human being. The soul is not a perfection of body taken as something complete and separate from all its forms. The author’s wording refers to both points.
“Without any condition” means body as a general kind, not body considered as something already complete on its own.

Material body means body taken as something complete and separate from whatever is joined to it. What is joined to this kind of body cannot be its first perfection. Generic body, by contrast, is taken without excluding what is joined to it; it can be united with that further feature and made complete by it. That is how the soul is a first perfection of body as a general kind.

“Natural body” can mean a body that is not a mathematical abstraction, a body that is not an imaginal or intermediate-world body, or a body that is not made by craft. The last meaning is intended here.

The phrase “natural body” excludes forms such as the forms of a bed or other made objects. The author also wants to exclude the way a pilot’s soul completes a ship or a king’s soul completes a city. Such a soul is not the soul of the ship or city, because a thing’s first perfection—its true form and distinguishing feature—must be one with it. Even if one grants that a pilot’s soul completes a ship or a king’s soul completes a city, it is a perfection of an artificial body, not a natural one. If the entire ship or city together with the pilot or king were treated as one thing, that whole would not exist as one thing in the world. Existence and unity go together.

“Tools” may be read as an adjective describing the natural body, or as a description of the soul, which acts through tools. Either reading is possible; the first is preferable. The phrase “not every natural body” qualifies “natural body,” not “perfection.”

“Immaterial” is not being used here in its strict technical sense of “not existing in matter,” which would exclude plant and animal souls. It means that the soul is higher in its own level of existence than matter: its existence is not identical with the matter it informs.

The intellect and soul, simply as intellect or soul, do not directly move the heavens. Yet the motion is still governed by the soul, because nature is subject to it. Otherwise, all motion would be called natural, since nature is the immediate agent in every case. Aristotle therefore calls the motions of the heavenly bodies natural.
The heavenly powers are distinct from the four elements, which are subject to coming-to-be and passing away.
The theoretical and practical intellects in their potential or material stage.
There is no potential intellect in the heavens, since all the perfections of a heavenly body are already actual except for its positions.

The intellect that forms part of the definition of “rational”—as in “a rational being is a soul with intellect”—does not mean a fully actual intellect. It means the shared capacity that includes both intellect in potential and intellect in act. Otherwise, a human being would not be rational while the intellect remained only potential.

These are images received from things that already have images. They affect an organ and the vital spirit, as when the two eyes or the vital spirit are affected at the meeting point of vision. This kind of reception does not occur in the heavens. The images there are not received from human beings, horses, cattle, and other things; they are the source and foundation of such images. They are like causal forms that precede what they cause, as God’s knowledge precedes what is known. There is no affected organ there, since the heavens have no eyes, ears, or anything like them. The forms flow to the heavenly spheres from within.

This responds to Avicenna’s claim that this kind of perception does not occur in the heavens. Intellectual perception—the highest kind of knowledge through mental forms—is enough to call the heavens living, even if they do not sense or do not have forms impressed in them. If Avicenna means that sensation cannot occur there because no organ passively receives an image, the reply is the next argument. The author does not explicitly answer Avicenna’s claim that the heavenly intellect is actual while an animal’s is only potential. A better answer is that “living” means a being that can perceive and act; it does not require perception to be fully actual or passively received. One might ask why “power” can have two meanings here, when the soul’s definition was not allowed to use a word with two unrelated meanings. The reason is that “power” was equivocal between two categories: acting and being acted upon. These categories are different kinds of possible things, with no shared essence. Perception, by contrast, is grounded in existence. Knowledge, life, will, and power follow existence and are identical with it in their reality, each according to its own level. Perception is therefore one shared idea, even though one kind of perception is active and another receptive.

The author’s point is that the concept of a body’s being able to act does not rule out its being preceded by another state. It differs from “perfection” in the definition above, which cannot be preceded by another perfection. These concepts have opposite meanings, so the aspects they express cannot be identical in the soul.

“A ship’s being useful” means its being in a condition where it can perform its function. The concept does not exclude the possibility that an earlier condition was needed; it does not mean that such a condition must have been needed.

At first, the sentence might seem to mean that, just as a body’s being able to burn and its having heat are one thing, a body’s being able to carry out the actions of life and its soul are also one thing, though the soul came first. That is not the point. The author means that the soul and the body’s ability to perform the actions of life are not one thing. As the ship’s usefulness may be preceded in time, the body’s ability to perform the actions of life is preceded by the soul. The body’s ability to burn and the heat in it, by contrast, are the same thing: its ability to burn is simply its having heat.

Avicenna says in The Healing that a body’s being able to perform an action or have a quality can happen in two ways. In the first, some other thing in the body produces that action or quality. For example, the ship’s being useful depends on the pilot. One must prove that the pilot and the ship’s usefulness are distinct. In the second, nothing other than that state exists in the body: for someone who identifies heat with the body’s being able to burn, the heat in the body is exactly that capacity. At first glance, the soul might seem to be like heat in this second sense, but that cannot be right. The soul is not the same as a body’s being able to produce the acts of life.
“Rather” marks a stronger claim: we establish that life must be preceded by another condition, not merely that it might be.
